reason: The formula and the S x IV / sqrt(252) break-even are both on the page. The 'profits only if realized exceeds implied' wording is too strong. The source says the identity holds only in a simplified model (fixed IV, continuous hedging, no financing). It says discrete hedges, costs, changing IV and gamma, and financing add terms, so realized above implied is neither necessary nor sufficient for net profit. It also calls the break-even a daily standard-deviation scale, not a rule.
found: In the simplified fixed-IV, continuous-hedging, zero-financing model this isolates the variance component of P&L. Discrete hedges, transaction costs, changing IV/gamma and financing add terms, so future realized variance exceeding the initial IV does not by itself guarantee net profit.
suggested_fix: In a simplified model (fixed IV, continuous hedging, no financing or costs), a delta-hedged long straddle's P&L over a short interval is approximately one-half gamma times S squared times (realized variance minus implied variance) times dt, so its variance component is positive when realized volatility exceeds the implied volatility paid; discrete hedging, costs, IV changes and financing add other terms. The ATM straddle's daily break-even move is roughly S times IV divided by the square root of 252.

reason: Fidelity states every part of the claim. The cited long-straddle page compares the two strategies: a strangle's break-evens are further apart, it has a greater chance of losing 100%, and it is more sensitive to time decay. But cited quote SQ2-7 is about straddles. The statement that a long strangle has positive vega is on Fidelity's long-strangle page, so that URL should be added as a citation.
found: When volatility falls, long strangles decrease in price and lose money. In the language of options, this is known as “positive vega.” ... The first disadvantage is that the breakeven points for a strangle are further apart than for a comparable straddle. Second, there is a greater chance of losing 100% of the cost of a strangle if it is held to expiration. Third, long strangles are more sensitive to time decay than long straddles.
